embeddedCheckAllFourChoicesAndRationaleR.question: During IV diuresis, a patient remains congested but is breathing more easily, has adequate urine output and stable perfusion, and has a small creatinine increase. Which interpretation best supports the next decision?
choices: Reassess the full trajectory; a functional filtration change may permit continued decongestion with monitoring
Diagnose tubular injury from the creatinine change alone and stop every diuretic
Continue the same regimen even if hypotension and oliguria subsequently develop
Use weight loss alone to decide that congestion has resolved
embeddedCheckAllFourChoicesAndRationaleR.rationale: Improvement with adequate perfusion and urine response makes a functional change possible, so the overall trajectory guides treatment. Creatinine alone does not diagnose tubular damage. New hypotension or oliguria requires reassessment rather than unconditional continuation. Weight loss alone does not exclude residual congestion.

individualQuestionReview.question: During decongestion, a patient has improving edema and breathing, maintained urine output and perfusion, and a small creatinine rise. How should that rise be interpreted?

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: It may reflect a functional change in filtration; it does not by itself prove tubular injury
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Definite tubular injury, regardless of the treatment response
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Proof that no kidney injury is possible during further diuresis
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Proof that all residual congestion has resolved
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

individualQuestionReview.rationaleReviewed: The response and adequate perfusion make a functional filtration change possible, while continued assessment is necessary. A creatinine rise alone cannot establish tubular injury. It also cannot exclude later injury. Kidney chemistry is not proof that congestion has resolved.

individualQuestionReview.source: ACC2025 full clinical-trajectory and congestion tables/figures; ROSE selected secondary-analysis possibility and limitations
individualQuestionReview.question: A patient receiving intensive diuresis develops new hypotension, cool extremities, sharply falling urine output, and a rising creatinine. What is the most appropriate response?

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Promptly reassess perfusion, volume, drug exposure, and other causes of kidney dysfunction, then adjust treatment to the findings
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Continue unchanged because every rise during diuresis is a benign functional change
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Increase fluid removal based solely on the creatinine rise
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Withhold reassessment until a discharge creatinine is available
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

individualQuestionReview.rationaleReviewed: The new hypoperfusion and oliguria require urgent reassessment and individualized treatment. The reassuring interpretation from successful, well-perfused decongestion cannot be applied automatically here. Creatinine alone does not justify more fluid removal. Waiting until discharge misses a worsening trajectory.

individualQuestionReview.source: ACC2025 full clinical-trajectory and congestion tables/figures; ROSE selected secondary-analysis possibility and limitations
individualQuestionReview.question: A congested patient has a creatinine increase after several IV loop doses. Which assessment best distinguishes a tolerated filtration change from a concerning trajectory?

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Compare congestion response, perfusion, pressure, urine output, serial chemistry, relevant urinalysis, and nephrotoxic exposure
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Use the creatinine value alone to decide whether the kidney is structurally injured
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Use a single normal blood-pressure reading to exclude kidney hypoperfusion or venous congestion
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Ignore the medication timeline if weight has fallen
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

individualQuestionReview.rationaleReviewed: The combined trajectory provides context for both filtration and injury. Creatinine alone does not identify the mechanism. One cuff pressure cannot characterize tissue flow or venous pressure. Weight change cannot replace review of medication and nephrotoxin exposure.

individualQuestionReview.source: ACC2025 full clinical-trajectory and congestion tables/figures; ROSE selected secondary-analysis possibility and limitations
individualQuestionReview.question: Why can automatically stopping decongestion for a small creatinine rise be harmful when congestion is improving but still present and perfusion remains adequate?

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: It may leave clinically important residual congestion untreated without demonstrating kidney benefit
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: A small creatinine rise proves the patient needs a large saline bolus
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Residual venous congestion cannot affect kidney function
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: It establishes that the diuretic must be continued unchanged under every later circumstance
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

individualQuestionReview.rationaleReviewed: A small rise can accompany effective decongestion, and residual congestion still matters; decisions need the whole trajectory. The rise does not prove depletion or justify a saline bolus. Venous congestion can impair renal function. This reasoning also does not support unconditional continuation if perfusion or urine output worsens.

individualQuestionReview.question: A patient with decompensated heart failure and edema has a low serum sodium. Which interpretation should guide the initial workup?

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Water retention with reduced effective arterial filling is possible, but tonicity and depletion or other causes still need evaluation
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Edema proves sodium depletion and makes isotonic fluid the default treatment
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Heart failure establishes SIADH without further evaluation
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: The sodium concentration alone distinguishes water excess from excessive diuresis
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

individualQuestionReview.rationaleReviewed: Heart failure can promote water retention despite reduced effective arterial filling, while diuresis and other mechanisms can also cause hyponatremia. Edema does not establish sodium depletion or an automatic fluid prescription. Heart failure is not itself a diagnosis of SIADH. The sodium number alone cannot determine tonicity or volume mechanism.

individualQuestionReview.question: A patient with confirmed hypotonic hyponatremia develops seizures attributed to the sodium disorder. What takes priority?

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Urgent monitored treatment of the neurologic emergency while the cause is evaluated
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Delay treatment until every urine study has returned
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Start tolvaptan as the urgent neurologic rescue drug
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Use outpatient fluid restriction alone and defer hospital monitoring
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

individualQuestionReview.rationaleReviewed: Serious neurologic symptoms require urgent monitored correction and ongoing investigation. A complete urine workup must not delay emergency care. The tolvaptan label excludes patients who need sodium raised urgently for serious neurologic symptoms. Outpatient restriction alone does not address this emergency.

individualQuestionReview.source: 2014 hyponatraemia full relevant diagnostic/expanded-volume text and native figure6
individualQuestionReview.question: A patient with low sodium has recently received a loop diuretic and also has kidney dysfunction. How should urine sodium and osmolality be used?

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Interpret them with a contemporaneous blood sample, tonicity, clinical findings, diuretic timing, and kidney function
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Diagnose SIADH from an elevated urine sodium alone
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Assume diuretic use excludes all other causes of hyponatremia
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Ignore serum osmolality because urine values establish hypotonicity by themselves
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

individualQuestionReview.rationaleReviewed: Paired measurements help, but diuretics and impaired kidney function complicate interpretation. An elevated urine sodium alone does not establish SIADH. Diuretics may contribute without excluding another cause. Serum tonicity still needs assessment; urine values cannot establish it alone.

individualQuestionReview.source: 2014 hyponatraemia full relevant diagnostic/expanded-volume text and native figure6
individualQuestionReview.question: A patient with hypotonic hyponatremia is markedly congested, without evidence of true volume depletion. What error should be avoided?

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Giving isotonic fluid automatically just because the serum sodium is low
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Reviewing symptoms and the correction trajectory during cause-specific treatment
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Considering whether diuretics or intake contribute to the sodium disorder
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Reassessing perfusion as congestion is treated
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

individualQuestionReview.rationaleReviewed: An automatic isotonic-fluid prescription can aggravate congestion when water excess is the mechanism. Symptom and correction monitoring are appropriate. Diuretics and intake deserve review because mechanisms can overlap. Perfusion reassessment remains necessary during decongestion.

individualQuestionReview.question: A patient taking digoxin develops low potassium and magnesium during loop-plus-thiazide diuresis. Why does this combination deserve prompt attention?

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Electrolyte depletion increases rhythm risk and susceptibility to digoxin toxicity
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Low potassium protects against digoxin toxicity
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Low magnesium makes the potassium result clinically unimportant
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: The absence of edema proves that electrolyte monitoring can stop
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

individualQuestionReview.rationaleReviewed: Potassium and magnesium depletion can increase electrical instability and digoxin susceptibility. Low potassium does not provide protection. Low magnesium adds risk and can hinder potassium correction. Improved edema does not establish safe electrolyte concentrations or remove the need for monitoring.

individualQuestionReview.source: Private RxPrep native476,478,479,481–483 full relevant drug/electrolyte tables and text
individualQuestionReview.question: A patient needs potassium replacement after diuresis and also has kidney impairment and an MRA-containing regimen. What is the safest planning principle?

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Individualize replacement and repeat monitoring using kidney function, urine output, rhythm risk, ongoing losses, and potassium-raising therapy
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Use the same replacement amount for every low potassium result
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Assume an MRA eliminates the need to treat or monitor hypokalemia
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Increase replacement automatically as kidney function declines
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

individualQuestionReview.rationaleReviewed: Replacement must account for the current deficit and the risks of accumulation and potassium-raising medicines. A fixed amount ignores severity and changing clearance. An MRA does not remove an existing deficit or the need to monitor. Declining kidney function is not a reason to increase replacement automatically.

individualQuestionReview.source: Private RxPrep native476,478,479,481–483 full relevant drug/electrolyte tables and text
individualQuestionReview.question: After repeated potassium replacement during intensive diuresis, which reassessment best supports the next replacement decision?

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Serial potassium and magnesium, renal function and urine output, ECG or rhythm findings, acid-base state, drug exposure, and ongoing losses
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Only the original potassium value before any replacement
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Only the amount of weight lost since admission
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Only the absence of muscle symptoms
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

individualQuestionReview.rationaleReviewed: Current chemistry and clearance, electrical risk, medicines, and losses inform whether more replacement is appropriate. The original result cannot describe the response to doses already given. Weight loss does not measure potassium or magnesium. Clinically important abnormalities can occur without muscle symptoms.

individualQuestionReview.source: Private RxPrep native476,478,479,481–483 full relevant drug/electrolyte tables and text
individualQuestionReview.question: Potassium remains low despite replacement in a patient receiving diuretics. What should be considered next alongside continued severity-appropriate care?

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Assess magnesium deficiency and other ongoing losses while reviewing kidney function and the replacement plan
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Keep increasing potassium indefinitely without rechecking magnesium or renal function
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Assume a normal magnesium result from before diuresis excludes a current deficit
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Assume repeated replacement guarantees that potassium has normalized
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

individualQuestionReview.rationaleReviewed: Magnesium deficiency can impede potassium correction, so it belongs in the assessment together with ongoing losses and clearance. Unchecked escalation can cause harm as physiology changes. A magnesium result from before subsequent losses does not exclude a current deficit. Repeated doses require reassessment; they do not prove normalization.

individualQuestionReview.question: Under the U.S. tolvaptan hyponatremia label, which situation meets the sodium-related eligibility conditions after tonicity and volume classification?

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Hypervolemic or euvolemic hyponatremia below 125 mEq/L, or a less marked reduction that is symptomatic and has resisted fluid restriction
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Any congested heart-failure patient with a normal serum sodium
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: A less marked sodium reduction that is asymptomatic and has not undergone fluid-restriction assessment
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Serious neurologic symptoms requiring an urgent sodium rise
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

individualQuestionReview.rationaleReviewed: The hypervolemic or euvolemic hyponatremia option matches the labeled alternatives, but still requires a full appropriateness and safety review. Congestion with normal sodium is not this indication. A less marked reduction requires both symptoms and resistance to fluid restriction. Urgent neurologic rescue is specifically outside labeled use.

individualQuestionReview.source: Current generic tolvaptan full label boxed warning,sections1,2,4,5,7,8.6/8.7,14.2,17;native relevant pages actually read
individualQuestionReview.question: After interruption, a patient is being considered for restarting tolvaptan for hyponatremia. What plan follows the U.S. label?

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Reinitiate in hospital with close sodium and volume monitoring, access to water, and avoidance of fluid restriction during the first 24 hours
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Restart at home because a previous tolerated course eliminates the hospital requirement
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Enforce tight fluid restriction immediately to maximize the initial sodium rise
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Check sodium only at the next routine monthly visit
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

individualQuestionReview.rationaleReviewed: The hospital requirement applies to reinitiation as well as the first start. Prior tolerance does not remove rapid-correction risk. Initial fluid restriction can increase that risk, and the label advises avoiding it for 24 hours while allowing drinking in response to thirst. Monthly-only sodium review is inadequate during initiation.

individualQuestionReview.source: Current generic tolvaptan full label boxed warning,sections1,2,4,5,7,8.6/8.7,14.2,17;native relevant pages actually read
individualQuestionReview.question: Before a tolvaptan decision, which finding is a labeled contraindication rather than simply a reason for individualized review?

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Anuria
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Any reduction in kidney function, regardless of urine production
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: Stable use of a potassium-raising medicine, by itself
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: A remote, resolved episode of hyponatremia, by itself
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

individualQuestionReview.rationaleReviewed: Anuria is a contraindication and offers no expected benefit. Kidney impairment is not equivalent to anuria, although renal function must inform appropriateness. Potassium-raising medicines call for potassium monitoring rather than being a universal contraindication by themselves. A remote episode does not determine current eligibility; current disease and risks need evaluation.

individualQuestionReview.question: A plan proposes indefinite tolvaptan solely to improve survival in a congested heart-failure patient. What concern most directly challenges that plan?

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: The hyponatremia label limits exposure to 30 days because of liver risk, and the studied heart-failure outcome benefit was not demonstrated
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: A rise in sodium automatically proves a survival benefit
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: The liver-exposure limit applies only when sodium fails to rise
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

choicesIndividuallyReviewed.text: The medicine removes the need for disease-directed heart-failure treatment and monitoring
choicesIndividuallyReviewed.singleBestAnswerContext: Case-specific; source and rationale distinguish this choice

individualQuestionReview.rationaleReviewed: The proposed purpose and duration conflict with the labeled limits and outcome evidence. Raising sodium does not establish improved survival. A sodium response does not waive the 30-day liver-risk limit. Tolvaptan does not replace disease-directed therapy or clinical and laboratory monitoring.
